title: Randomized truthful unrelated-machine scheduling
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors as \(m\to \infty\), the function \(R(m)\): the infimum worst-case expected-makespan approximation ratio achievable by truthful-in-expectation mechanisms with monetary payments for m unrelated machines and an arbitrary number of indivisible jobs. The infimum ranges over all mechanisms, without a computational or communication restriction. In particular, is \(R(m)=\Theta (1)\)?
definitions: There are \(m\ge 2\) machines and \(n\ge 1\) jobs. Machine i privately knows a vector \(t_{i}\in R_{\ge 0}^{n}\); processing a set S costs it \(\sum_{j\in S}t_{ij}\). Every entry is finite. A direct-revelation mechanism maps reported vectors \(b=(b_{1},\ldots ,b_{m})\) to a distribution over assignments \(\sigma :\{1,\ldots ,n\}\to \{1,\ldots ,m\}\) and payments to the machines. Jobs are indivisible and every job is assigned exactly once. Let \(x_{ij}(b)=\Pr [\sigma (j)=i]\) and let \(p_{i}(b)\) be the finite expected payment to i. Risk-neutral utility is payment minus true processing cost. Truthfulness in expectation means that for every i, true \(t_{i}\), alternative report \(b_{i}\) and fixed reports \(b_{- i}, p_{i}(t_{i},b_{- i})- \sum_{j} t_{ij}x_{ij}(t_{i},b_{- i})\ge p_{i}(b_{i},b_{- i})- \sum_{j} t_{ij}x_{ij}(b_{i},b_{- i})\). This is a dominant-strategy condition against arbitrary fixed reports, without a prior on types. The makespan is \(C(\sigma ,t)=\max _{i} \sum_{j:\sigma (j)=i}t_{ij}\), and \(\operatorname{OPT}(t)=\min _{\sigma} C(\sigma ,t)\). For each m, consider a family \(M=(M_{m,n})_{n\ge 1}\) satisfying this incentive condition for every n and report profile. Its ratio is \(\sup _{n,t:\operatorname{OPT}(t)>0} E[C(M_{m,n}(t),t)]/\operatorname{OPT}(t)\), and it must also have expected makespan zero when \(\operatorname{OPT}(t)=0\). \(R(m)\) is the infimum of those ratios. Random assignments may be correlated across jobs. No budget balance, bound on transfers, individual-rationality constraint, anonymity, task independence or efficient representation is imposed. Since only expected utilities matter, payments can equivalently be deterministic amounts \(p_{i}(b)\).
answer_criterion: Give an explicit asymptotic scale \(f(m)\) and universal constants \(a,b>0\) such that a \(f(m)\le R(m)\le b f(m)\) for all sufficiently large m, with matching incentive-theoretic lower bounds and mechanisms achieving the upper scale. A constant-factor mechanism for all numbers of machines and jobs would settle the target as \(\Theta (1)\). Showing only that \(R(m)\) is unbounded would rule out that possibility but would not determine the requested asymptotic order without matching bounds. Restrictions on the mechanism class or input distributions must not be silently added.
why: Determine the asymptotic efficiency loss caused solely by truthful multidimensional incentives when randomization and payments are fully available.

importance.reason: The central randomized counterpart of the resolved Nisan–Ronen conjecture, with a constant-versus-linear gap independent of computational restrictions.

progress.text: Mu’alem–Schapira establish the lower bound \(2- 1/m\) for randomized scheduling, including truthfulness in expectation; the full version gives the extended weak-monotonicity argument.
Lu–Yu give improved universally truthful two-machine mechanisms and a general truthful-in-expectation upper bound \((m+5)/2\); the linear lower bound in their WINE paper assumes task independence.
Kuryatnikova–Vera sharpen bounds for a restricted scale-free mechanism class on two machines, including an almost tight two-job calculation; first published 30 May 2019.
Christodoulou–Koutsoupias–Kovács post the proof that deterministic truthful scheduling has optimal ratio m, while recording the distinct randomized bounds.
The deterministic Nisan–Ronen proof is published online in the Journal of the ACM; its theorem does not cover truthful-in-expectation randomization.

status_note: The Nisan–Ronen proof, now published in JACM in February 2026, resolves only deterministic truthful mechanisms. Its randomized discussion records \(2- 1/m\) and \((m+5)/2\) bounds. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no matching unrestricted randomized bounds; results for task-independent mechanisms, fractional objectives, Bayesian types or no-payment models do not resolve this formulation.

context_blocks.text: A machine has a reason to exaggerate how long jobs take: receiving fewer jobs reduces its work. Payments are intended to counteract that incentive while keeping the overall schedule short. The private information is a whole vector, since a machine may be fast on one job and slow on another. A single speed parameter would describe a different and substantially more structured scheduling model.

The optimization objective creates the difficulty. Minimizing total processing cost can be implemented truthfully by a VCG mechanism, which assigns each job to a cheapest machine. But total cost and makespan differ. The largest load is at most the total cost, while the total cost of an optimal makespan schedule is at most m times its makespan. Thus this familiar truthful rule gives an m-approximation. Without incentive constraints and with unlimited computation, one could simply choose an optimal assignment.

Christodoulou, Koutsoupias and Kovács prove that the factor m is unavoidable for deterministic truthful mechanisms, resolving the Nisan–Ronen conjecture. Their result appeared as a 2023 preprint and in the Journal of the ACM in February 2026. It is an unconditional incentive restriction, independent of computational hardness. The paper’s related-work discussion expressly separates the unresolved randomized setting from this deterministic conclusion.

There are two different ways to randomize truthfully. A universally truthful mechanism draws a deterministic truthful mechanism before seeing the reports. Truthfulness in expectation only asks that honest reporting maximize expected utility; individual random outcomes need not implement truthful rules on their own. Universal truthfulness implies the latter condition, but the definition in this card permits the larger class. Mu’alem and Schapira nevertheless prove a lower bound of \(2- 1/m\) even for that larger class.

Randomization already helps when there are two machines. Lu and Yu’s STACS 2008 mechanism is universally truthful and beats the deterministic factor two. Their later WINE 2008 paper gives a truthful-in-expectation mechanism with ratio \((m+5)/2\) for general m, using a fractional allocation and a suitable rounding procedure. The improvement is substantial in its leading constant, but the guarantee still grows linearly with the number of machines.

The WINE paper also proves a lower bound \((m+1)/2\) for its task-independent class. A mechanism in the full question may use all reported jobs together and correlate their assignments. Consequently, a lower bound that treats each job separately does not close the gap between the general constant lower bound and linear upper bound. Whether such global dependence can change the asymptotic answer is part of what makes this question interesting.

Expected makespan must be distinguished from the largest expected machine load. Consider m identical machines and m unit jobs. Assigning all jobs to one uniformly random machine gives expected load one on every machine, yet the makespan is always m. Assigning one job per machine has makespan one. Thus the same marginal load target can conceal a factor-m difference in the objective. A truthful fractional solution, or an argument that controls only marginal probabilities, needs a valid rounding analysis before it yields a guarantee for this card.

Fine numerical results for small cases illuminate mechanisms without settling the asymptotic problem. Kuryatnikova and Vera obtain almost matching bounds near 1.505996 for two machines and two jobs within a class of randomized monotone scale-free algorithms. Their paper does not identify the optimal ratio over every truthful-in-expectation mechanism, every job count and a growing number of machines. Both the input restriction and mechanism restriction matter when interpreting the result.

The final question is whether allowing random outcomes fundamentally reduces the price of truthful multidimensional cost reporting. A constant answer would permit useful load balancing despite unrestricted private processing times. A growing lower bound would show that even risk-neutral incentives and unrestricted payments cannot recover the efficiency available to a scheduler who knows the true costs. Matching bounds would quantify that loss as a function of system size.

sentences: Unrelated-machine scheduling assigns jobs to machines with privately known processing times for each job.
The question asks for the optimal expected-makespan approximation achievable by truthful-in-expectation mechanisms as the number of machines grows.
Random assignments can correlate decisions across jobs while payments discourage strategic misreporting.
A constant ratio would show that randomization overcomes the large incentive cost known for deterministic mechanisms.
The saved review emphasizes that maximum expected load is different from expected maximum load, and restricted task-independent lower bounds do not settle the unrestricted mechanism class.
